item.title: Will we observe dark matter as a particle or a wave?
item.description: We have arguably already discovered dark matter, says columnist Chanda Prescod-Weinstein. To observe it, we will need to figure out whether we expect it to act like a particle or a wave.

item.title: Solving the gallium anomaly: New calculation may explain neutrino shortfall without invoking new particles
item.description: Glimpses of the "gallium anomaly" were first seen in the mid-1990s, but it was first clearly discovered and stated in 2007 by neutrino physicist Carlo Giunti of Italy. The problem is simple to state but potentially very important: about 20% fewer electron neutrinos were seen to be captured by gallium nuclei than expected.

item.title: Rare particle decays hint at deviations from Standard Model predictions
item.description: Studying rare processes is part and parcel of particle physics, providing stringent tests of the Standard Model. At the recent International Conference on High Energy Physics (ICHEP), the CMS and LHCb collaborations presented their latest research into one such process: the transformation of a beauty quark into a strange quark, a muon and the oppositely charged antimuon (b→sμ⁺μ⁻).

item.title: Triplet of ‘Ghostly’ Galaxies Hints at What Dark Matter Is — and Isn’t
item.description: A collision may have left these galaxies without dark matter. That spells trouble for alternative gravity theories. The post Triplet of ‘Ghostly’ Galaxies Hints at What Dark Matter Is — and Isn’t first appeared on Quanta Magazine

item.title: New research shows a neutrino laser is impossible
